blocks.text: A random variable turns the uncertain outcome of an experiment into a number that ordinary arithmetic can work with. This lesson covers discrete random variables specifically, ones whose possible values can be listed out one by one, like the number of heads in a series of coin flips or the class label a model assigns to an image, and the probability mass function that describes how likely each of those values is.

blocks.alt: A random variable mapped through a probability mass function that sums to 1
blocks.caption: From a random experiment to a probability mass function

blocks.text: 1. What a Random Variable Is

A random variable is a function that assigns a number to every possible outcome of a random experiment. Flipping a coin does not itself produce a number, but defining a random variable X that equals 1 for heads and 0 for tails turns the flip into something arithmetic can operate on directly, adding, averaging, and comparing outcomes numerically.

The word variable is slightly misleading, a random variable is not unknown in the way an algebra variable like x in an equation is unknown, it is a fixed rule for assigning numbers, the randomness lives entirely in which outcome the underlying experiment happens to produce.

code.content:
import numpy as np
coin_flip_outcome = np.random.choice(["heads", "tails"])
X = 1 if coin_flip_outcome == "heads" else 0
print(X)

blocks.title: A concrete example
blocks.content: Rolling a die and defining X as the number showing face up turns the physical die roll into a random variable taking values 1 through 6, letting arithmetic like averaging many rolls together apply directly to the outcome.

blocks.text: 2. Discrete Versus Continuous Random Variables

A discrete random variable can only take a value from a countable list, like the integers 0, 1, 2, and so on, with clear gaps between consecutive possible values. Rolling a die, counting emails in an inbox, or counting the number of correct predictions out of 100 all produce discrete random variables.

This is in direct contrast to a continuous random variable, covered in its own lesson later in this module, which can take any value along a continuous range, like a person exact height, with no gaps between possible values at all.

blocks.text: A helpful test for telling the two apart is to ask whether it makes sense to list every possible value one after another, 0, 1, 2, and so on works fine for a discrete count, but no such list exists for a continuous quantity like exact height, since there are infinitely many possible values between any two heights no matter how close together they are.
3. The Probability Mass Function

The probability mass function, almost always abbreviated PMF, assigns a probability to every possible value a discrete random variable can take, written P(X equals x). It is the discrete counterpart to what section 3 in the continuous random variables lesson calls a probability density function, but unlike a density, a PMF value is itself a genuine probability.
For a fair six sided die, the PMF assigns exactly one sixth to each of the values 1 through 6, and zero to every other number, since rolling a 7 or a 2.5 is simply not possible on a standard die.

code.content:
pmf = {1: 1/6, 2: 1/6, 3: 1/6, 4: 1/6, 5: 1/6, 6: 1/6}
print(pmf[4])   # 0.1667, the probability of rolling a 4

blocks.text: A PMF can be written as a formula, a table, or plain code as shown above, all three are equivalent descriptions of the exact same underlying random variable, the choice of representation is purely a matter of convenience for the calculation at hand.
4. Every PMF Must Sum to 1

Because a random variable must take exactly one of its possible values on any given trial, summing the PMF over every possible value must give exactly 1, a direct application of the sum-to-1 rule covered in the probability rules lesson.

code.content:
import numpy as np
values = list(pmf.keys())
probs = list(pmf.values())
assert np.isclose(sum(probs), 1.0)   # the whole PMF must sum to 1

blocks.title: A concrete example
blocks.content: A biased coin with P(heads) equal to 0.7 must have P(tails) equal to 0.3, since heads and tails are the only two possible outcomes and the PMF for this random variable, 0.7 plus 0.3, must sum to exactly 1.

blocks.text: This sum-to-1 requirement is exactly what makes a PMF a valid probability distribution rather than just an arbitrary list of non negative weights, any list of non negative numbers can be turned into a valid PMF by dividing each one by the total sum, a process called normalizing.
5. Bernoulli Random Variables

A Bernoulli random variable is the simplest possible discrete random variable, it takes only two values, usually written 0 and 1, representing failure and success. A single coin flip, a single spam or not spam classification, and a single click or no click on an advertisement are all naturally modeled as Bernoulli random variables.
A Bernoulli random variable is fully described by a single number p, the probability of success, its PMF is simply P(X equals 1) equals p and P(X equals 0) equals 1 minus p.

code.content:
from scipy import stats
p_success = 0.3
bernoulli = stats.bernoulli(p_success)
print(bernoulli.pmf(1))   # 0.3
print(bernoulli.pmf(0))   # 0.7

blocks.text: The name Bernoulli honors the mathematician who first studied this simplest possible random variable formally, and the same name reappears throughout statistics, a Bernoulli trial is simply one instance of flipping such a two outcome random variable.
6. Binomial Random Variables

A binomial random variable counts the number of successes across a fixed number of independent Bernoulli trials, each with the same success probability p. Counting the number of heads in 10 independent coin flips is the textbook example, but a click through count across 500 independent ad impressions is exactly the same structure.

A binomial random variable is fully described by two numbers, n, the number of trials, and p, the success probability of each trial, and its PMF requires counting how many distinct sequences of successes and failures produce a given total, which is where the combinatorial coefficient in the formula below comes from.

code.content:
from scipy import stats
n, p_success = 10, 0.5
binomial = stats.binom(n, p_success)
print(binomial.pmf(5))   # probability of exactly 5 heads in 10 flips
print(binomial.pmf(10))  # probability of all 10 flips landing heads

blocks.text: The full binomial PMF formula multiplies three pieces together, the number of distinct orderings that produce exactly k successes out of n trials, p raised to the power k for the successes, and 1 minus p raised to the power n minus k for the failures, and scipy computes all three pieces internally whenever pmf is called.

blocks.text: 7. The Dice Roll as a Discrete Random Variable

A single fair die roll is a useful example because every one of its six outcomes shares exactly the same probability, a case called a uniform discrete random variable. This flat PMF makes it an easy first example for visualizing what a PMF actually looks like as a shape.

blocks.alt: PMF of a fair six sided die, flat across all six outcomes
blocks.caption: Every outcome of a fair die shares exactly the same probability, one sixth

blocks.text: Because every face shares exactly the same probability, this particular PMF is called a discrete uniform distribution, the discrete counterpart to the continuous uniform distribution briefly mentioned in the continuous random variables lesson.
8. Plotting a PMF

A PMF is almost always plotted as a bar chart, one bar per possible value, with bar height equal to the probability of that value, rather than as a smooth curve. The gaps between bars in a PMF plot are meaningful, they visually reinforce that only the labeled values are actually possible, unlike the smooth continuous curves covered in the next lesson.

code.content:
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt
values = [1, 2, 3, 4, 5, 6]
probs = [1/6] * 6
plt.bar(values, probs)
plt.xlabel('Die outcome')
plt.ylabel('Probability')
plt.show()

blocks.text: A common plotting mistake is connecting the bar tops with a smooth line, which visually implies values in between the bars are also possible, exactly the discrete versus continuous confusion flagged in section 2, keeping the bars separate and unconnected avoids sending that wrong signal.
9. Expected Value of a Discrete Random Variable

The expected value of a discrete random variable is a weighted average of its possible values, each value weighted by its own PMF probability, written as the sum over every value x of x times P(X equals x). For a fair die, this comes out to 3.5, the long run average result across a very large number of rolls, even though 3.5 is not itself a possible single outcome.

code.content:
expected_value = sum(x * p for x, p in pmf.items())
print(expected_value)   # 3.5

blocks.text: Expectation and variance are covered in far greater depth in their own dedicated lesson elsewhere in this module, this section only introduces the definition needed to make sense of discrete random variables as a whole.

Expected value describes only the center of a distribution, it says nothing about how spread out the possible outcomes are around that center, which is exactly what variance, covered in the dedicated expectation and variance lesson, is built to describe.
10. Discrete Random Variables in AI Practice

A classification model output, once passed through softmax, is itself best understood as the PMF of a discrete random variable over the set of possible class labels, each class assigned a probability, and every one of those probabilities summing to exactly 1, mirroring the sum-to-1 rule from section 4 exactly.

items: A language model choosing its next token is sampling from a discrete random variable whose possible values are every token in its vocabulary, each assigned a probability by the model output PMF.
A recommendation system choosing which one of several candidate items to show a user is drawing from a discrete random variable over the candidate item identifiers.
Counting the number of correctly classified examples out of a fixed test set batch is a binomial random variable, directly matching the structure covered in section 6.

blocks.text: Discrete token sampling is worth calling out specifically, generation temperature and top-k or nucleus sampling settings all work by reshaping the discrete PMF over the vocabulary before a single token is drawn from it.

Beam search and greedy decoding in language model generation are two different strategies for choosing which value to commit to from a discrete random variable over the vocabulary, one keeping several candidate sequences alive at once and the other always taking the single highest probability token.
11. Cumulative Distribution of a Discrete Random Variable
11.1 Adding Up the PMF

The cumulative distribution function, or CDF, of a discrete random variable gives P(X is less than or equal to x), found by adding up every PMF value at or below x. For a fair die, the CDF at 3 is P(X equals 1) plus P(X equals 2) plus P(X equals 3), which comes to one half.

code.content:
cdf_at_3 = sum(p for x, p in pmf.items() if x <= 3)
print(cdf_at_3)   # 0.5

blocks.text: Unlike a PMF, which jumps up and down between individual values, a CDF for a discrete random variable always climbs in a series of steps and never decreases, reaching exactly 1 once x covers every possible value.

A CDF is often more convenient than a raw PMF whenever the question being asked is about a range of values rather than a single exact value, for instance finding the probability of rolling a 3 or lower is a direct CDF lookup rather than three separate PMF lookups added by hand.
12. Joint and Marginal Discrete Random Variables

When two discrete random variables are considered together rather than separately, the natural extension is a joint probability mass function, exactly the joint probability tables covered in the joint probability lesson elsewhere in this module, and summing out one variable from such a table recovers the marginal PMF of the other, matching the marginal probability idea from that same lesson.

For example, jointly modeling both a predicted class label and a predicted confidence bucket for a classifier produces a small joint PMF table over those two discrete random variables together, with the class label marginal recoverable by summing out the confidence bucket dimension.
13. A Worked Example

A quality control process inspects light bulbs coming off a production line, each bulb independently has a 5 percent chance of being defective. Out of a batch of 4 bulbs, let X be the number of defective bulbs, a binomial random variable with n equal to 4 and p equal to 0.05.

code.content:
from scipy import stats
n, p_success = 4, 0.05
X = stats.binom(n, p_success)
for k in range(n + 1):
    print(k, round(X.pmf(k), 4))
print('sum:', round(sum(X.pmf(k) for k in range(n + 1)), 4))   # 1.0

blocks.text: Notice the probabilities decline sharply as the number of defective bulbs increases, and the full PMF still sums to exactly 1, confirming no possible outcome was left out of the table.

blocks.title: Sanity checking with the complement rule
blocks.content: P(at least one defective bulb) can be found quickly as 1 minus P(zero defective bulbs), which is 1 minus 0.8145, giving 0.1855, matching the complement rule from the probability rules lesson rather than requiring every other row of the table to be added by hand.

blocks.text: 14. Common Mistakes

items: Treating a discrete random variable value as though any number in between two listed values were also possible, when the whole point of discreteness is that only the listed values can occur.
Forgetting to verify a constructed PMF actually sums to 1, especially after manually adjusting individual probabilities without rebalancing the rest.
Confusing the expected value of a random variable with its most likely single outcome, the two frequently differ, a fair die expected value of 3.5 is not even a possible roll.
Applying the binomial PMF formula to trials that are not actually independent or do not share the same success probability, silently producing an incorrect answer.
Mixing up a PMF with a CDF, reading a cumulative less-than-or-equal-to value as though it described a single exact outcome instead.

blocks.text: A related trap is assuming a binomial random variable applies whenever there are exactly two outcomes per trial, when in fact the trials also need to be independent and share the same success probability, a condition worth checking explicitly rather than assumed.
15. Practice: Build and Check a PMF

A weighted six sided die is built so that landing on 6 is twice as likely as landing on any of the other five faces, which are all equally likely to each other. Find the full PMF and confirm it sums to 1.

code.content:
base = 1  # relative weight for faces 1 through 5
six_weight = 2  # relative weight for face 6
total_weight = base * 5 + six_weight
pmf_weighted = {i: base / total_weight for i in range(1, 6)}
pmf_weighted[6] = six_weight / total_weight
print(pmf_weighted)
print(round(sum(pmf_weighted.values()), 6))   # 1.0

blocks.text: Once the PMF checks out, try computing the expected value of this weighted die using the same weighted sum formula from section 9, and compare it against the fair die expected value of 3.5, it should come out noticeably higher.
As a further check, compute P(X is greater than or equal to 5) for the weighted die using the CDF idea from section 11, and confirm it matches 1 minus the CDF evaluated at 4.
Key Takeaway

A discrete random variable turns a countable set of outcomes into numbers, and its probability mass function assigns a genuine probability to each one, with every value summing to exactly 1. Bernoulli and binomial random variables are the two most common building blocks, and both extend naturally into the classification and token sampling settings that show up constantly in applied AI.

The next lesson in this module, continuous random variables, relaxes the countable-list assumption made throughout this lesson, replacing sums with integrals and a PMF with a probability density function, while keeping the same underlying goal of describing how likely different outcomes are.
